graders.name: identities
graders.evidence:
Here are the 7 reply styles. I haven't changed anything.

| Style | Best for | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **lcd** | You pass Claude's replies on to others, read on a phone, or work in a room with mixed skills. | Anyone can relay it. It forces one real example. It's the cheapest to read. | The glosses are noise for peers. Length caps squeeze the reasoning. It's weak for design debates. |
| **bluf** | Managers and decision-makers who read only the first three lines. | Fastest to read. Decision-ready. | Loses nuance. Assumes you know the domain. |
| **engineer** | Senior developers reading in an IDE or terminal. | No filler. Precise names. | Unreadable for non-technical readers. Terse replies can hide assumptions, so an evidence line is mandatory. |
| **teacher** | Juniors, onboarding, or learning an unfamiliar codebase. | Builds understanding. Fewer repeat questions. | Slower and costs more tokens. Can drift into lecture. |
| **minimal** | Power users iterating fast, and one-line tasks. | Fast, with no overhead. | Hides risk and assumptions, so a risk line is mandatory. Wrong for anything that needs a decision. |
| **plain** | Business owners, operators, and support staff who will never open the code. | Non-technical people can act on it. | Not implementable on its own. Pair it with `engineer` when code is involved. |
| **memo** | Design decisions, counter-proposals, and post-mortems. | The reasoning is visible and debatable. | Long. Wrong for fixes and quick questions. |

**Where to start, by role:**

| Who you are | Start with | Switch to |
|---|---|---|
| Developer reading in an IDE | engineer | `minimal` to iterate fast, `memo` for a design decision, `teacher` in an unfamiliar codebase |
| Senior or lead reviewing others' work | engineer (or `bluf` for status) | `memo` for architecture calls |
| Founder or idea person building with Claude | lcd | `memo` for product decisions, `plain` when forwarding to customers, `engineer` when you go into the code yourself |
| Developer who forwards replies or reads on a phone | lcd | `engineer` when heads-down in code |
| Manager or product owner who decides | bluf | `memo` for big decisions, `lcd` when relaying to a mixed team |
| Non-technical (ops, support, marketing, owner) | plain | `lcd` once a few terms are familiar |
| Student, junior, or learning a codebase | teacher | `engineer` once fluent |
| Analyst, researcher, or writer | memo for findings, `bluf` for status | `lcd` for a mixed audience |
| Trainer or consultant explaining to clients | lcd | `teacher` for lessons, `plain` for client-facing text |
| Power user with nobody to relay to | minimal | `engineer` when something breaks, `memo` before a big change |

The table is per situation, not for life. Styles are instructions, not enforcement, so they aren't guaranteed. Errors, warnings, and destructive-action confirmations keep full content in every style.

To use one, run `/reply-style <name>` to install and switch. `/reply-style try <name>` applies it to this conversation only and writes no files. Tell me your role if you'd like a recommendation.
